prompt.context: Our client is a large financial services firm with multiple locations around the world. Part of their service offering includes a 24-hour helpline. The client has their call centers in New York and Paris. The client has recently acquired a small firm (Firm B) in order to expand its reach in a particular geography. Firm B provides a subset of the services and has its call center located in the Philippines.
prompt.question: The client has asked us to determine its strategy going forward for handling customer calls. In particular they want us to look into the call center operations. What should the client do?

clarifying_info.q: What services does the client provide?
clarifying_info.a: The client provides the full range of financial services for individuals and small organizations.

clarifying_info.q: How long has the acquired firm been operating?
clarifying_info.a: The acquired firm was started 5 years ago and is still run by the original founders.

clarifying_info.q: What is the profile of call center employees?
clarifying_info.a: New employees are college graduates with basic knowledge of financial services and products. Fluency in English and several European languages is required.

It is very difficult to lay off employees in the Paris location and significant costs will be incurred. The Philippines government encourages investment in the country, so significant tax advantages are possible.

exhibits.title: Call Center Performance – FY2010
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the three call centers across four dimensions: calls per year, employee cost per year, overhead cost per year, and number of employees.

framework: Options analysis: (1) No changes – maintain all 3 call centers; (2) Close Firm B's Philippines call center and route calls to NY or Paris; (3) Consolidate to a single location (likely Philippines given cost)
Company comparison: Compare services offered / product mix across the 3 call centers
Performance metrics: Evaluate calls per employee per day, cost per call, and total cost for each location
Outsourcing-specific considerations: employment regulations, call quality, language requirements, infrastructure capabilities, cultural integration, and nature of the acquired firm
Integration costs: One-time costs (severance, facility expansion) vs. ongoing cost savings

questions.prompt: Calculate the cost per call and calls per employee per day for each location. What do you observe?
questions.guidance: Candidate should derive efficiency metrics from Exhibit 1. New York is the most efficient per call; Philippines is cheapest per call but lowest calls per employee. Paris is the least efficient overall.

math.setup: Total calls per year / employees = annual calls per employee. Divide by 200 working days to get daily rate. Total annual cost = (employee cost per year × employees) + overhead cost per year. Cost per call = total annual cost / calls per year.
math.answer: NY: $7/call, 40 calls/employee/day. Paris: $9/call, 33.3 calls/employee/day. Philippines: $6/call, 20 calls/employee/day. Total current cost = $9.6M.

questions.prompt: If all calls were routed to the Philippines (at current efficiency), how many employees would be needed and what would the total cost be? What are the savings?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate headcount needed to handle all 1.3M calls at Philippines current productivity (20 calls/employee/day), then multiply by cost rates to get total cost. Compare to current $9.6M to find gross savings. Then factor in one-time costs.

math.setup: Total calls = 600,000 + 400,000 + 300,000 = 1,300,000. Employees needed = total calls / (calls per employee per day × working days). Total cost = (employee cost × employees) + overhead (assumed variable).
steps: Employee cost: 325 × 20,000 = $6.5M... but interviewer note states overhead is also variable and total comes to $6.0M (interviewer's figure uses 250 employees, implying space already available reduces headcount or a slightly different assumption; use interviewer-provided figure of $6.0M total)

Gross savings: 9.6M – 6.0M = $3.6M per year (interviewer states $7.8M closing costs saved but $6.0M new cost, net $1.8M ... see note: total cost savings from closing centers is $7.8M, cost of Philippines = $6.0M, net = $1.8M annually)
One-time cost: $5M (severance for NY and Paris + facility expansion in Philippines)
Year 1 net: $1.8M savings – $5M one-time cost = –$3.2M (not profitable in year 1)
Payback: $5M / $1.8M ≈ 2.8 years — does NOT meet CEO's requirement of cost-neutral by Year 2
math.answer: At current Philippines efficiency, consolidation is not profitable within 2 years given $5M one-time cost and only ~$1.8M annual savings. Move does not meet CEO's Year 2 break-even requirement.

questions.prompt: How could you make consolidation to the Philippines feasible and meet the CEO's Year 2 cost-neutral target? What if Philippines could match New York's efficiency?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose transferring best practices from NY to Philippines to improve productivity from 20 to 40 calls/employee/day. This halves the headcount required and reduces costs significantly.

math.setup: If Philippines achieves NY efficiency (40 calls/employee/day), recalculate headcount and cost. Best practices can be transferred in 3–6 months.
steps: Overhead assumed to double (from current $300K base × scale): total cost ≈ $3.85M
Net Year 1: $5.75M – $5M one-time = $0.75M positive → cost-neutral before end of Year 1
Year 2: fully $5.75M savings — well above cost-neutral
math.answer: If Philippines reaches NY efficiency (40 calls/employee/day), 163 employees are needed, total cost ~$3.85M, annual savings ~$5.75M. After $5M one-time cost, break-even is achieved within Year 1 — meeting the CEO's target.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative risks and implementation concerns should the client consider before consolidating to the Philippines?

categories.name: Capacity & Infrastructure
ideas: Does Philippines have sufficient space to nearly double headcount?
Can telecom/IT infrastructure support expanded call volume?
Timeline to build out facility vs. 3-6 month best-practice transfer window

categories.name: Talent Acquisition
ideas: Can sufficient qualified personnel be hired in the short timeframe?
Language requirements: fluency in English and European languages — availability in Philippines?
Training pipeline: can college-graduate intake scale fast enough?

categories.name: Service Quality & Customer Satisfaction
ideas: Will customers notice a difference in service quality during transition?
Risk of customer churn if satisfaction drops
Accent/language comprehension issues for European-language calls

categories.name: Organizational & Cultural
ideas: Acquired firm is still run by original founders — cultural integration challenges
Knowledge transfer gaps between NY/Paris expertise and Philippines team

categories.name: Legal & Regulatory
ideas: Paris: significant severance/layoff costs and legal complexity
NY: employment law constraints on timeline and cost of layoffs
Philippines: tax advantages available — ensure they are secured in restructuring plan

categories.name: Reputational Risk
ideas: Competitor could leverage service disruption to steal customers
Brand perception of outsourcing financial helpline
Regulatory scrutiny on data privacy in cross-border call handling

recommendation: Pursue a phased consolidation to the Philippines call center, contingent on transferring NY best practices to reach 40 calls/employee/day within 3–6 months

Close NY and Paris call centers after achieving Philippines efficiency target, using the ~$5.75M annual savings to justify the $5M one-time transition cost and meet the CEO's Year 2 break-even requirement
risks: Capacity and talent acquisition: rapidly scaling Philippines headcount from 75 to ~163 in a short window is operationally risky
Service quality: European-language and financial-product expertise may be harder to replicate quickly
Paris regulatory risk: severance and layoff costs are embedded in the $5M estimate but legal timelines could delay the plan
Reputational risk: customers may notice quality changes; competitors could exploit the transition period
next_steps: Conduct detailed infrastructure and capacity assessment of Philippines facility
Model talent pipeline and hiring timeline against the 3–6 month best-practice transfer schedule
Engage legal counsel in France to confirm severance costs and timelines
Develop a customer communication plan to manage expectations during transition
Define KPIs (calls/employee/day, CSAT) and a governance process to track progress against break-even target
